exemplars.title: StoryEnsemble: Enabling Dynamic Exploration & Iteration in the Design Process with AI and Forward-Backward Propagation
exemplars.why: Four workflow stages—personas, problems, solutions, and scenarios—occupy one interconnected environment, with forward and backward propagation making their shared state and cross-stage consistency mechanism explicit.
exemplars.over_the_runner_up: StoryEnsemble ranks over SnapClass because bidirectional propagation demonstrates a substantive shared-state mechanism, rather than relying mainly on the fact that several activities occur around the same artifact.

exemplars.title: SnapClass: An AI-Enhanced Classroom Management System for Block-Based Programming
exemplars.why: The evidence explicitly replaces platform switching with one interface for viewing code, tracking progress, grading, and giving feedback, all naturally anchored to the same student-work state.
exemplars.over_the_runner_up: SnapClass ranks over Dynamite because it supplies both halves of the pattern claim—previous platform switching and consolidated stages—while Dynamite leaves the prior separation and precise state binding unstated.

exemplars.title: Dynamite: Real-Time Debriefing Slide Authoring through AI-Enhanced Multimodal Interaction
exemplars.why: A single real-time workspace couples classroom analytics with slide authoring, allowing interpretation and instructional intervention to occur within one application shell.
exemplars.over_the_runner_up: Dynamite ranks over QueryGenie because its real-time coupling of analytics to immediate authoring more clearly demonstrates the consequential value of consolidation than the comparatively established edit-run-inspect query loop.

notes: I retained the consensus top three but reordered SnapClass above Dynamite. SnapClass is structurally more complete because its quotation explicitly identifies the former platform-switching problem and names four consolidated stages; Dynamite clearly names two integrated regions but only implies how analytic state becomes addressable during slide authoring. No score adjustment exceeds 0.3. The main evidentiary weakness is that all selections rest on single quotations: StoryEnsemble does not establish that the stages previously occupied separate tools, while SnapClass and Dynamite do not describe the exact on-screen state-binding operations. SnapClass’s shared state is inferred from the stages operating on the same student work, and Dynamite’s is inferred from real-time integration rather than directly demonstrated.
